sources.text: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying,
They came into the house and saw the young child with Mary, his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Opening their treasures, they offered to him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.
There were shepherds in the same country staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock.

inputs.question: How do Matthew and Luke differ in their accounts of Jesus’ birth?

answer:
The supplied passages highlight different scenes:

- Matthew places the birth “in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod” and focuses on “wise men from the east” who come to Jerusalem [S1]. They later come “into the house,” worship the child and offer gold, frankincense, and myrrh [S2].
- Luke describes Mary wrapping her son in bands of cloth and laying him “in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn” [S3], and then turns to shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night [S4].

In these passages Matthew does not mention the shepherds and Luke does not mention the wise men. Many readers treat the two accounts as complementary, each Gospel selecting different events; others focus on their distinct emphases.

sources.text: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
He lifted up his eyes to his disciples, and said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for God’s Kingdom is yours.

Interpreters differ on how to relate Matthew’s and Luke’s beatitudes. Some see Luke stressing literal poverty and Matthew spiritual humility; others see one teaching given on different occasions, or summarised differently by each Gospel writer.

inputs.question: Compare the first beatitude in Matthew and Luke.

answer: Matthew has “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven” [S1]. Luke has Jesus look at his disciples and say, “Blessed are you who are poor, for God’s Kingdom is yours” [S2]. So Matthew speaks of the “poor in spirit” in the third person, while Luke addresses “you who are poor” directly [S1][S2]. The commentary notes that interpreters differ on how to relate the two: some see Luke stressing literal poverty and Matthew spiritual humility, while others see one teaching given on different occasions or summarised differently [S3].

sources.text: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us today our daily bread.
He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. Give us day by day our daily bread.

inputs.question: List the differences between the Lord’s Prayer in Matthew and in Luke.

answer:
- Introduction: Matthew has “Pray like this” [S1]; Luke has “When you pray, say” [S2].
- Kingdom and will: Matthew reads “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done” [S1]; Luke reads “May your Kingdom come. May your will be done” [S2].
- Bread: Matthew asks “Give us today our daily bread” [S1]; Luke asks “Give us day by day our daily bread” [S2].
- Shared opening: both begin “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy” [S1][S2].

sources.text: Now after the Sabbath, as it began to dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.
But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they and some others came to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared.
Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.

inputs.question: Who went to the tomb on the first Easter morning according to the Gospels?

answer:
All three Gospel passages place the visit on the first day of the week, around dawn:

- Matthew: “Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb” as it began to dawn [S1].
- Luke: “they and some others” came at early dawn, bringing the spices they had prepared [S2]. The supplied verse does not name the women; “they” refers back to earlier verses that are not included here.
- John: Mary Magdalene went “while it was still dark” and saw that the stone had been taken away [S3].

Mary Magdalene is named in both Matthew and John [S1][S3].

sources.text: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

inputs.question: How do Ephesians and Colossians describe forgiving one another?

answer: Both letters ground forgiving others in the forgiveness believers have received. Ephesians says, “be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” [S1]. Colossians says, “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do,” and places forgiveness alongside “bearing with one another” when someone has a complaint [S2]. Ephesians frames it as God forgiving “in Christ” [S1], while Colossians speaks of Christ forgiving [S2].
